--- title: "Part 1 — Python MapReduce Without Hadoop" subtitle: "Hands-on MapReduce Programming with Python" format: ipynb: default jupyter: python3 execute: echo: true warning: false error: true --- # Part 1 — Python MapReduce Without Hadoop ## Learning Objectives In this practical, you will learn the MapReduce programming model by implementing it entirely in Python. By the end of this practical, you will be able to: - understand the MapReduce programming model; - implement a Mapper; - implement a Shuffle operation; - implement a Reducer; - process text data using MapReduce; - process CSV data using MapReduce; - perform counting, summation, averaging, and ranking; - compare MapReduce with Pandas; - process progressively larger datasets; - understand why distributed frameworks such as Hadoop are useful. > **Important:** Hadoop is **not used in Part 1**. You will first understand the MapReduce programming model using Python alone. --- # 1. Environment Setup ## 1.1 Activate the Conda Environment Before starting this practical, activate the `demo` Conda environment. Run the following command in your terminal: ```bash conda activate demo ```` If the environment does not exist yet, create it using: ```bash conda create -n demo python=3.11 -y conda activate demo ``` --- ## 1.2 Install Required Python Packages Run the following command in your terminal: ```bash pip install pandas numpy matplotlib seaborn requests openpyxl ``` The main packages used in this practical are: | Package | Purpose | | ------------ | ------------------------------ | | `pandas` | Dataset loading and comparison | | `numpy` | Numerical operations | | `matplotlib` | Visualization | | `seaborn` | Visualization | | `requests` | Downloading datasets | | `openpyxl` | Reading Excel datasets | The first demonstration uses only Python's standard library. --- ## 1.3 Verify the Environment Run the following Python cell. ::: {#69968c8b .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import sys import pandas as pd import numpy as np import matplotlib import seaborn as sns print("Python version:", sys.version) print("Pandas version:", pd.__version__) print("NumPy version:", np.__version__) print("Matplotlib version:", matplotlib.__version__) print("Seaborn version:", sns.__version__) print("\nEnvironment is ready!") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Python version: 3.11.13 (main, Jun 5 2025, 08:14:07) [Clang 14.0.6 ] Pandas version: 3.0.5 NumPy version: 2.4.6 Matplotlib version: 3.11.1 Seaborn version: 0.13.2 Environment is ready! ``` ::: ::: --- # 2. Understanding the MapReduce Model Before writing the first program, understand the basic MapReduce workflow. ```text INPUT DATA | v +----------+ | MAPPER | +----------+ | v KEY-VALUE PAIRS | v +----------+ | SHUFFLE | +----------+ | v GROUPED VALUES | v +----------+ | REDUCER | +----------+ | v OUTPUT ``` The three important stages are: ### Mapper Converts input records into key-value pairs. ### Shuffle Groups values belonging to the same key. ### Reducer Aggregates the grouped values. For example, for Word Count: ```text Input: Python Hadoop Python Mapper: Python -> 1 Hadoop -> 1 Python -> 1 Shuffle: Python -> [1, 1] Hadoop -> [1] Reducer: Python -> 2 Hadoop -> 1 ``` In Hadoop, the framework performs the Shuffle phase. In this practical, you will implement the Shuffle phase yourself so that you can understand exactly what happens. --- # 3. Demo 1 — Word Count ## Objective You will implement your first complete MapReduce program. The problem is: > **Count how many times each word occurs in a text dataset.** You will implement: ```text Mapper ↓ Shuffle ↓ Reducer ``` --- ## 3.1 Create a Small Dataset Run the following cell. ::: {#b16825b7 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} text = """ Python is simple Python is powerful Hadoop processes big data Python processes data Hadoop and Python work together """ print(text) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Python is simple Python is powerful Hadoop processes big data Python processes data Hadoop and Python work together ``` ::: ::: --- ## 3.2 Save the Dataset Run: ::: {#5489577f .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} with open("word_count_input.txt", "w") as file: file.write(text) print("Dataset saved as word_count_input.txt") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Dataset saved as word_count_input.txt ``` ::: ::: --- ## 3.3 Read the Dataset Run: ::: {#b1133fa5 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} with open("word_count_input.txt", "r") as file: lines = file.readlines() print("Number of lines:", len(lines)) for line in lines: print(repr(line)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Number of lines: 6 '\n' 'Python is simple\n' 'Python is powerful\n' 'Hadoop processes big data\n' 'Python processes data\n' 'Hadoop and Python work together\n' ``` ::: ::: --- # 4. Implement the Mapper The Mapper should convert every word into: ```text (word, 1) ``` For example: ```text Python Python Hadoop ``` becomes: ```text ("python", 1) ("python", 1) ("hadoop", 1) ``` Run the following cell. ::: {#d22a76fa .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} def word_count_mapper(lines): mapped_data = [] for line in lines: words = line.strip().lower().split() for word in words: mapped_data.append((word, 1)) return mapped_data ``` ::: --- ## 4.1 Run the Mapper ::: {#95723ed9 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} mapped_data = word_count_mapper(lines) print("Mapper output:\n") for key, value in mapped_data: print(key, "->", value) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Mapper output: python -> 1 is -> 1 simple -> 1 python -> 1 is -> 1 powerful -> 1 hadoop -> 1 processes -> 1 big -> 1 data -> 1 python -> 1 processes -> 1 data -> 1 hadoop -> 1 and -> 1 python -> 1 work -> 1 together -> 1 ``` ::: ::: ### Observe You should see output similar to: ```text python -> 1 is -> 1 simple -> 1 python -> 1 is -> 1 powerful -> 1 ... ``` The Mapper does not calculate the final count. It only produces key-value pairs. --- # 5. Implement the Shuffle The Shuffle phase groups values having the same key. For example: ```text python -> 1 python -> 1 python -> 1 ``` becomes: ```text python -> [1, 1, 1] ``` Run: ::: {#24c36a29 .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} from collections import defaultdict def shuffle(mapped_data): grouped_data = defaultdict(list) for key, value in mapped_data: grouped_data[key].append(value) return grouped_data ``` ::: --- ## 5.1 Run the Shuffle ::: {#f9049a32 .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} grouped_data = shuffle(mapped_data) print("Shuffle output:\n") for key, values in grouped_data.items(): print(key, "->", values) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Shuffle output: python -> [1, 1, 1, 1] is -> [1, 1] simple -> [1] powerful -> [1] hadoop -> [1, 1] processes -> [1, 1] big -> [1] data -> [1, 1] and -> [1] work -> [1] together -> [1] ``` ::: ::: --- # 6. Implement the Reducer The Reducer receives: ```text key -> [values] ``` and calculates the final result. For Word Count: ```text python -> [1, 1, 1] ``` becomes: ```text python -> 3 ``` Run: ::: {#bfc1aea4 .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} def word_count_reducer(grouped_data): result = {} for key, values in grouped_data.items(): result[key] = sum(values) return result ``` ::: --- ## 6.1 Run the Reducer ::: {#3fef0e84 .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} word_count_result = word_count_reducer(grouped_data) print("Reducer output:\n") for key, value in word_count_result.items(): print(key, "->", value) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Reducer output: python -> 4 is -> 2 simple -> 1 powerful -> 1 hadoop -> 2 processes -> 2 big -> 1 data -> 2 and -> 1 work -> 1 together -> 1 ``` ::: ::: --- # 7. Sort the Results Run: ::: {#f3d580c5 .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} sorted_word_count = sorted( word_count_result.items(), key=lambda item: item[1], reverse=True ) for word, count in sorted_word_count: print(f"{word:15} {count}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` python 4 is 2 hadoop 2 processes 2 data 2 simple 1 powerful 1 big 1 and 1 work 1 together 1 ``` ::: ::: --- # 8. Build a Complete MapReduce Function You have implemented Mapper, Shuffle, and Reducer separately. Now combine them into one function. ::: {#e8308ff1 .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} def map_reduce( data, mapper_function, reducer_function ): # MAP mapped = mapper_function(data) # SHUFFLE grouped = shuffle(mapped) # REDUCE result = reducer_function(grouped) return result ``` ::: --- ## 8.1 Execute the Complete Pipeline ::: {#3b68341a .cell execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code} result = map_reduce( lines, word_count_mapper, word_count_reducer ) for key, value in sorted( result.items(), key=lambda item: item[1], reverse=True ): print(f"{key:15} {value}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` python 4 is 2 hadoop 2 processes 2 data 2 simple 1 powerful 1 big 1 and 1 work 1 together 1 ``` ::: ::: --- # 9. Visualize the Word Count Run: ::: {#6fda8208 .cell execution_count=14} ``` {.python .cell-code} import matplotlib.pyplot as plt words = [item[0] for item in sorted_word_count] counts = [item[1] for item in sorted_word_count] plt.figure(figsize=(10, 5)) plt.bar(words, counts) plt.xlabel("Word") plt.ylabel("Frequency") plt.title("Word Frequency") plt.xticks(rotation=45) plt.tight_layout() plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](session-06-big-data-part1_files/figure-html/cell-15-output-1.png){width=952 height=472} ::: ::: --- # 10. Check Your Understanding Answer these questions before continuing. ### Question 1 What does the Mapper produce? ### Question 2 Why is the value `1` in the Word Count Mapper? ### Question 3 What does Shuffle do? ### Question 4 What does the Reducer calculate? ### Question 5 What would happen if the Mapper produced: ```text python -> 5 ``` instead of: ```text python -> 1 ``` --- # 11. Demo 2 — Real CSV Dataset ## Objective You will now move from a manually created text dataset to a real dataset downloaded from the Internet. We will use the **Online Shoppers Purchasing Intention** dataset from the UCI Machine Learning Repository. The dataset contains online shopping sessions and includes information such as visitor type, browsing activity, and whether a purchase was made. --- ## 11.1 Download the Dataset Run: ::: {#4a3c4b96 .cell execution_count=15} ``` {.python .cell-code} import requests from pathlib import Path url = ( "https://archive.ics.uci.edu/" "ml/machine-learning-databases/" "00468/online_shoppers_intention.csv" ) filename = Path("online_shoppers_intention.csv") if not filename.exists(): response = requests.get(url) response.raise_for_status() filename.write_bytes(response.content) print("Dataset downloaded successfully.") else: print("Dataset already exists.") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Dataset already exists. ``` ::: ::: --- ## 11.2 Load the Dataset ::: {#d081c26a .cell execution_count=16} ``` {.python .cell-code} import pandas as pd df = pd.read_csv( "online_shoppers_intention.csv" ) df.head() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=16} ```{=html}

Demo 2 — Counting by Visitor Type ## Problem Answer the following question: > **How many sessions belong to each VisitorType?** First solve the problem using Pandas. --- ## 12.1 Pandas Solution ::: {#a5330062 .cell execution_count=20} ``` {.python .cell-code} pandas_counts = df["VisitorType"].value_counts() pandas_counts ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=20} ``` VisitorType Returning_Visitor 10551 New_Visitor 1694 Other 85 Name: count, dtype: int64 ``` ::: ::: This is our reference solution. --- # 13. Implement the Mapper The Mapper should produce: ```text VisitorType -> 1 ``` Run: ::: {#8261d40b .cell execution_count=21} ``` {.python .cell-code} def visitor_type_mapper(df): mapped = [] for visitor_type in df["VisitorType"]: mapped.append( (visitor_type, 1) ) return mapped ``` ::: --- ## 13.1 Execute the Mapper ::: {#6decb6c6 .cell execution_count=22} ``` {.python .cell-code} visitor_mapped = visitor_type_mapper(df) print("First 20 Mapper records:\n") for item in visitor_mapped[:20]: print(item) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` First 20 Mapper records: ('Returning_Visitor', 1) ('Returning_Visitor', 1) ('Returning_Visitor', 1) ('Returning_Visitor', 1) ('Returning_Visitor', 1) ('Returning_Visitor', 1) ('Returning_Visitor', 1) ('Returning_Visitor', 1) ('Returning_Visitor', 1) ('Returning_Visitor', 1) ('Returning_Visitor', 1) ('Returning_Visitor', 1) ('Returning_Visitor', 1) ('Returning_Visitor', 1) ('Returning_Visitor', 1) ('Returning_Visitor', 1) ('Returning_Visitor', 1) ('Returning_Visitor', 1) ('Returning_Visitor', 1) ('Returning_Visitor', 1) ``` ::: ::: --- # 14. Shuffle the Data Use the Shuffle function created earlier. ::: {#0434858d .cell execution_count=23} ``` {.python .cell-code} visitor_grouped = shuffle( visitor_mapped ) for key, values in visitor_grouped.items(): print( key, "->", len(values), "records" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Returning_Visitor -> 10551 records New_Visitor -> 1694 records Other -> 85 records ``` ::: ::: --- # 15. Reduce the Data Use the existing Word Count reducer. ::: {#29c62367 .cell execution_count=24} ``` {.python .cell-code} visitor_counts = word_count_reducer( visitor_grouped ) visitor_counts ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=24} ``` {'Returning_Visitor': 10551, 'New_Visitor': 1694, 'Other': 85} ``` ::: ::: --- # 16. Compare MapReduce With Pandas ::: {#9463ea71 .cell execution_count=25} ``` {.python .cell-code} print("Pandas result:") print(pandas_counts.to_dict()) print("\nMapReduce result:") print(visitor_counts) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Pandas result: {'Returning_Visitor': 10551, 'New_Visitor': 1694, 'Other': 85} MapReduce result: {'Returning_Visitor': 10551, 'New_Visitor': 1694, 'Other': 85} ``` ::: ::: Check whether the results are identical: ::: {#8a8317a6 .cell execution_count=26} ``` {.python .cell-code} pandas_counts.to_dict() == visitor_counts ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=26} ``` True ``` ::: ::: You should get: ```text True ``` --- # 17. Demo 3 — Average Using MapReduce ## Objective You will now perform numerical aggregation. Answer: > **What is the average PageValues for each VisitorType?** The MapReduce operation is: ```text Mapper: VisitorType -> PageValues ↓ Shuffle: VisitorType -> [PageValue1, PageValue2, ...] ↓ Reducer: VisitorType -> Average(PageValues) ``` --- # 18. Implement the Mapper ::: {#41958493 .cell execution_count=27} ``` {.python .cell-code} def page_value_mapper(df): mapped = [] for _, row in df.iterrows(): visitor_type = row["VisitorType"] page_value = row["PageValues"] mapped.append( (visitor_type, page_value) ) return mapped ``` ::: --- # 19. Implement the Average Reducer ::: {#2320b5f2 .cell execution_count=28} ``` {.python .cell-code} def average_reducer(grouped_data): result = {} for key, values in grouped_data.items(): if len(values) > 0: result[key] = ( sum(values) / len(values) ) return result ``` ::: --- # 20. Execute MapReduce ::: {#d8e6000f .cell execution_count=29} ``` {.python .cell-code} average_result = map_reduce( df, page_value_mapper, average_reducer ) average_result ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=29} ``` {'Returning_Visitor': 5.006175700140938, 'New_Visitor': 10.77218748275915, 'Other': 18.19181222389411} ``` ::: ::: --- # 21. Verify Using Pandas ::: {#d0ee530f .cell execution_count=30} ``` {.python .cell-code} pandas_average = ( df.groupby("VisitorType")["PageValues"] .mean() ) pandas_average ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=30} ``` VisitorType New_Visitor 10.772187 Other 18.191812 Returning_Visitor 5.006176 Name: PageValues, dtype: float64 ``` ::: ::: Compare: ::: {#fd3fd176 .cell execution_count=31} ``` {.python .cell-code} print("MapReduce:") print(average_result) print("\nPandas:") print(pandas_average.to_dict()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` MapReduce: {'Returning_Visitor': 5.006175700140938, 'New_Visitor': 10.77218748275915, 'Other': 18.19181222389411} Pandas: {'New_Visitor': 10.77218748275915, 'Other': 18.191812223894118, 'Returning_Visitor': 5.006175700140934} ``` ::: ::: --- # 22. Demo 4 — Multiple Aggregations You will now use the same dataset to perform several MapReduce operations. The purpose of this exercise is to understand that the MapReduce model is **not limited to counting**. --- ## Task 1 — Count Revenue Sessions Determine how many sessions resulted in a purchase. The dataset contains the `Revenue` column. Use: ::: {#349a4758 .cell execution_count=32} ``` {.python .cell-code} df["Revenue"].value_counts() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=32} ``` Revenue False 10422 True 1908 Name: count, dtype: int64 ``` ::: ::: Now implement the same operation using MapReduce. --- ## Task 2 — Count Sessions by Month Use the `Month` column. Calculate: ```text Month -> Number of Sessions ``` --- ## Task 3 — Average Page Value by Month Calculate: ```text Month -> Average PageValues ``` --- ## Task 4 — Count Sessions by Visitor Type and Month This introduces a **composite key**. Instead of: ```text VisitorType -> Value ``` use: ```text (VisitorType, Month) -> Value ``` For example: ```text ("Returning_Visitor", "May") -> 1 ``` Implement the Mapper and Reducer yourself. --- # 23. Demo 5 — Medium Dataset ## Clickstream Data You will now move to a larger dataset. Use the **Clickstream Data for Online Shopping** dataset from the UCI Machine Learning Repository.
